c.tagline: Kazakhstan's futuristic steppe capital (formerly Nur-Sultan) of gleaming towers and bitter-cold winters.

taxi.fareNote: Most rides are booked through Yandex Go or inDrive with fixed upfront pricing; agree a fare before getting into any unmarked street taxi.

emergency.note: 112 is the unified emergency number reachable from any phone, including without SIM/credit; fire is 101.

hood_desc: The purpose-built modern heart of the capital on the left bank of the Ishim River, home to Astana's showpiece futuristic architecture — Bayterek Tower, the Akorda presidential palace, the Nur-Astana Mosque, and government ministries; the go-to base for first-timers and expats.
Part of the older right-bank city, with Soviet-era streets, bazaars, and everyday local life; more affordable and authentic than the glossy left bank.
A right-bank residential and transport district around the railway station and older neighborhoods, handy for budget stays and rail connections.
A newer district on the city's northern edge mixing residential blocks, shopping centers, and sports venues; a practical, quieter place to stay away from the tourist core.

water.note: Locals often boil or filter; bottled water is the safer choice for short stays.

transit.pay: Pay buses and the LRT by tapping a contactless bank card or phone at the reader, or with the local Tulpar transit card; single bus rides run about 110-250 tenge. Cash is generally not accepted on board.
transit.hours: The LRT and most buses run roughly 6:00 AM to 11:00 PM; Yandex Go and inDrive run 24/7 for late-night trips.
transit.note: Astana's automated LRT light-metro opened in May 2026, running elevated from the airport through the city; an extensive bus network and ride-hailing apps cover everywhere else — there is no traditional metro.

bus: Saparzhai Astana bus terminal for intercity coaches to Karaganda, Kokshetau, and beyond
train: Astana Railway Station and Nurly Zhol Station (Talgo and express rail to Almaty, Karaganda, and Petropavl)

transit.m: City bus #10 / #12 to the center (~40-50 min)
Astana LRT from the airport terminal into the city (opened 2026)

tip.r: Not traditionally required, but rounding up or leaving 5-10% at restaurants is increasingly common and appreciated where no service charge is included.

food.name: Beshbarmak
food.desc: The national dish: boiled horse or lamb laid over wide sheets of noodle with onion sauce, eaten with the hands and followed by a bowl of sorpa broth.

places.name: Qazaq Gourmet
places.note: Modern showcase of Kazakh cuisine in traditional decor; the easiest first beshbarmak.

places.name: Saksaul
places.note: Yurt-inspired dining room with a broad spread of Kazakh and Central Asian classics.

places.name: Alasha
places.note: Long-running Central Asian restaurant with private booths and generous meat platters.

food.name: Kazy and Horse Meat Platter
food.desc: Cured horse sausage made from rib meat, sliced thin and served cold with zhal and zhaya cuts; the centrepiece of any Kazakh celebration table.

places.name: Qazaq Gourmet
places.note: Serves the full horse-meat selection with explanations of each cut.

places.name: Artyom Bazaar meat rows
places.note: City market where kazy, zhaya and cured cuts are sold by weight; tasting is normal.

places.name: Saksaul
places.note: Cold meat plate as a starter before beshbarmak, good for a first try.

food.name: Kuyrdak
food.desc: Fried offal: liver, kidney, heart and lung of lamb or horse cooked down with onion, potato and fat until dark and rich, served straight from the pan.

places.name: Saksaul
places.note: Kuyrdak is one of the dishes the kitchen is specifically known for.

places.name: Qazaq Gourmet
places.note: Cleaner, more refined version if offal is unfamiliar territory.

places.name: Alasha
places.note: Traditional heavy version alongside grilled meats and pilaf.

food.name: Baursak
food.desc: Puffy squares of deep-fried dough piled high on the table, torn open and eaten with tea, butter, sour cream or honey at any hour.

places.name: Astykzhan
places.note: Local bakery chain, dependable for fresh baursak and Kazakh pastries to take away.

places.name: Artyom Bazaar bakery stalls
places.note: Market bakers frying baursak through the morning; buy them warm by the bag.

places.name: Qazaq Gourmet
places.note: Arrives automatically with the tea service alongside jams and cream.

food.name: Tandyr Samsa and Manti
food.desc: Clay-oven pastries stuffed with lamb and onion, and big steamed dumplings pleated shut and eaten with black pepper and sour cream.

places.name: Alasha
places.note: Central Asian menu strong on samsa, manti and pilaf cooked to order.

places.name: Artyom Bazaar food stalls
places.note: Tandyr ovens at the market turn out samsa all day for a fraction of restaurant prices.

places.name: Saksaul
places.note: Reliable sit-down version with a full range of Central Asian dumplings.

food.name: Shek-Shek and Irimshik
food.desc: Sweets from the steppe: honeyed fried dough shek-shek stacked into a mound, and irimshik, hard sun-dried curd eaten in nuggets with tea.

places.name: Artyom Bazaar dairy rows
places.note: Stalls of dried curd, kurt and irimshik sold loose; ask before you buy a kilo.

places.name: Qazaq Gourmet
places.note: Traditional sweets come out with the tea at the end of the meal.

places.name: Astykzhan
places.note: Bakery counters with shek-shek and other honeyed pastries by weight.

food.name: Kumys
food.desc: Fermented mare's milk, fizzy, sour and lightly alcoholic; the nomad drink of the steppe and still the standard toast at a Kazakh table.

places.name: Qazaq Gourmet
places.note: Serves kumys by the bowl with an explanation of how it is made.

places.name: Artyom Bazaar dairy rows
places.note: Bottled kumys sold cold by market traders, usually cheaper and stronger.

places.name: Saksaul
places.note: Traditional drinks list alongside the meat dishes they are meant to cut.

food.name: Shubat
food.desc: Fermented camel milk, thicker and creamier than kumys with a tangy finish; drunk chilled and long treated as a health tonic.

places.name: Artyom Bazaar dairy rows
places.note: The most reliable place to find fresh shubat, sold in bottles from the fridge.

places.name: Qazaq Gourmet
places.note: Restaurant version served cold in a bowl, easier than hunting the market.

places.name: Alasha
places.note: Usually stocks shubat and kumys alongside the Central Asian menu.

landmarks: Bayterek Tower
The capital's defining symbol, this 97-meter white tower crowned by a golden sphere offers panoramic views and embodies a Kazakh legend of the mythical Samruk bird.
Khan Shatyr Entertainment Center
Norman Foster's colossal transparent tent, the world's largest, shelters shops, gardens, and even an indoor beach from the fierce steppe winters.
Hazrat Sultan Mosque
One of Central Asia's largest mosques, its gleaming white marble and turquoise domes hold up to 10,000 worshippers beside Independence Square.
Nur-Alem (Museum of Future Energy)
The striking glass sphere built for Expo 2017 is the world's largest spherical building, housing eight floors of futuristic energy exhibits.
Palace of Peace and Reconciliation
Foster's 62-meter glass-and-granite pyramid hosts interfaith congresses and an opera hall, its apex glowing with doves painted across sunlit stained glass.
Ak Orda Presidential Palace
The president's blue-domed, white-columned residence anchors the monumental axis along the Ishim River, best photographed from across the water at dusk.
National Museum of the Republic of Kazakhstan
A vast modernist complex on Independence Square showcasing the golden treasures of Saka warriors, nomadic culture, and the capital's audacious rise.
Nur-Astana Mosque
A gift from Qatar, this elegant gold-domed mosque's 40-meter height symbolizes the Prophet's age when he received revelation.
Astana Opera
A neoclassical temple of culture with lavish interiors, staging world-class opera and ballet in one of the region's grandest theaters.
Ishim River Embankment
A landscaped riverside promenade linking the old and new cities, offering strollable views of Astana's audacious skyline and summer boat cruises.

train.note: Astana has two stations and it matters which one your ticket names: the older Astana-1 north of the centre handles most Russian-bound and classic long-distance trains, while Astana Nurly Zhol, about 10 km east and opened in 2017, takes the fast Talgo services, most Almaty trains and the China-bound service. Three trains a day run to Almaty, the quickest Talgo in around 13 hours and the classic sleepers in about 20, all overnight, with two-berth kupe places selling out early in summer. International services are sparse and slow - Moscow goes via Petropavlovsk and takes the better part of two days, Tashkent runs via Turkestan, and the weekly Ürümqi train has been intermittent since 2020, so confirm it is actually running before building a trip around it. Tickets open 45 days ahead on KTZ's site and app; foreign cards sometimes fail, in which case buy at the station with your passport.

intl.op: private coach and minibus operators — tickets at the Saparzhai terminal counters, no central online booking

bus.note: Long-distance coaches use the Saparzhai terminal next to Astana Nurly Zhol station, well east of the centre and reached by city bus or taxi. Domestic services fan out to Karaganda in about 3 hours, plus Pavlodar, Kokshetau and the lake resort of Borovoe/Burabay, which has no useful train and is the classic reason to take a bus here. Almaty by road is an 18-hour-plus ordeal that almost nobody chooses over the train. Cross-border coaches and shared minibuses to Bishkek, Tashkent and southern Russian cities are run by small private firms selling at the terminal windows rather than online, and Russian-bound travel needs a visa arranged well in advance.

ferry.note: Astana sits deep in the landlocked Kazakh steppe on the shallow Ishim River, which carries only summer sightseeing boats through the city parks and nothing scheduled. Kazakhstan's one passenger-carrying sea route is the Caspian ro-ro ferry from Aktau to Baku, roughly 2,000 km southwest and a journey in its own right.

half.name: Korgalzhyn Nature Reserve
half.blurb: UNESCO wetland reserve southwest of the city, a major breeding ground for flamingos and other migratory birds.

full.name: Burabay National Park (Borovoe)
full.blurb: Forested lake district nicknamed Kazakhstan's pearl of nature, with granite outcrops and hiking trails.

full.name: Karaganda
full.blurb: Industrial city with the Karlag Museum, documenting the Soviet-era gulag labor camp system centered here.
